new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisetla keeps the Swahili penultimate word stress as its default; a subset of words (the example is mwafrika 'an African', stressed on the antepenult after English 'African') take English stress placement instead. Heine 1973's sketch of Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili (his cover term for kisetla + kihindi) says the same from the other side: the word prosodeme (stress + slight lengthening, often raised pitch) is bound to the penultimate syllable, no distinctive prosodemes, with antepenult or final placement in some Arabic and English loanwords.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any recovered snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Muthiani: 'some words in Kisetla take the English stress' (mwafrika example, scanned-garbled). Heine 1973 fn. 73 (KPS): some words, mostly Arabic and English loans, carry the word prosodeme on the antepenult or final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Muthiani's subsection is 'Stress' under phonology; Heine's prosodeme is defined per 'Worteinheit' and is the basis of the phonological word in KPS). Heine adds phrase-level question and emphasis prosodemes on the same penultimate syllable, differing by tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All descriptions concern the pidgin Swahili used between European settlers and African workers in the Kenya highlands (Kisetla/Kisettla, 'Up-country' or 'Kitchen' Swahili), although Glottolog/Ethnologue place sett1235 [sta] in Zambia. Heine 1973's stress statement is for his 'Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili' (KPS), a cover term he defines as comprising kisetla (settler pidgin) and kihindi (Indian-shopkeeper pidgin, cf. cutc1238 Cutchi-Swahili), so it is not Kisetla-specific. Muthiani 1974 and Vitale 1980 describe Kisetla proper.

new_statements.quote: Das Vorkommen dieser drei Prosodeme ist an die vorletzte Silbe des Wortes gebunden. Distinktive Prosodeme konnten nicht festgestellt werden. Das ordinative Prosodem besitzt die Merkmale Druckakzent [...], leichte Längung des silbentragenden Elementes der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes [...], sowie [...] – aber nicht immer – gehobenen Ton. Da das ordinative Prosodem in jeder Worteinheit vorkommt, bildet es die Grundlage der phonologischen Definition des Wortes im KPS. [Fn. 73:] Bei einigen Wörtern kommt das ordinative Prosodem auf der drittletzten oder letzten Silbe des Wortes vor. Hierbei handelt es sich um Lehnwörter, die überwiegend dem Arabischen und dem Englischen entstammen.
new_statements.translation: The occurrence of these three prosodemes is bound to the penultimate syllable of the word. Distinctive prosodemes could not be established. The ordinative prosodeme has the features stress accent [i.e. increased sound pressure], slight lengthening of the syllable-bearing element of the penultimate syllable of the word [as a rule a vowel, occasionally a nasal consonant], and [...] – though not always – raised pitch. Since the ordinative prosodeme occurs in every word unit, it forms the basis of the phonological definition of the word in KPS. [Fn. 73:] In some words the ordinative prosodeme falls on the antepenultimate or the final syllable of the word. These are loanwords, mostly of Arabic and English origin.
new_statements.citation: Heine, Bernd. 1973. Pidgin-Sprachen im Bantu-Bereich (Kölner Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 3). Berlin: Reimer.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate) and as Muthiani 1974; adds that the prominence is non-contrastive, that it combines intensity, length and usually pitch, and that loanwords (Arabic and English, not only English as in Muthiani) can carry it on the antepenult or the final syllable. Heine's sketch is of Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili (KPS), his cover term for the kisetla (European-settler) and kihindi (Indian) dialects (§1.7), so it describes Kisetla at one remove.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries one non-distinctive 'ordinative prosodeme' (stress = intensity, plus slight lengthening of the penultimate syllable nucleus, usually but not always with raised pitch) on the penultimate syllable; it is culminative (one per word) and serves as the phonological definition of the word. Two further 'expressive' prosodemes (emphasis, question) are sentence-level and also sit on the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for KPS (the 'sekundärer Akzent auf der vorletzten Silbe' passage elsewhere in the book is about Lingala/Bangala, not KPS).
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 73: in some words the prosodeme falls on the antepenultimate or the final syllable; these are loanwords, mostly from Arabic and English. No distinctive (contrastive) prosodemes were found.
new_statements.identity_note: Heine 1973 does not describe Kisetla separately: §1.7 says the pidgin Swahili dialects arose 'zwischen Afrikanern und Europäern (kisetla) sowie zwischen Afrikanern und Indern (kihindi)', and the grammatical sketch (§4.2) is of Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili (KPS) as a cover variety; the stress statement therefore holds for Kisetla only insofar as Kisetla is part of KPS. Holm 1989 distinguishes Kisetla (European settlers, Kenyan highlands), Kihindi (Indian traders) and Lubumbashi Swahili but says nothing about Kisetla prosody. Both accent passages elsewhere in Heine ('automatischer Druckakzent auf der vorletzten Silbe jeden Wortes' = Fanagalo; 'tonaler Akzent (accent tonique) auf der ersten Silbe der Wurzel.. sekundärer Akzent auf der vorletzten Silbe' = Lingala/Bangala) are about other languages.
